query: Consider the following context: Materials capable of withstanding extreme environments open promising opportunities for nuclear fusion reactors. In that context, which material can be used for interlayer materials between W and CuCrZr, and why?

generation.hypothesis: A refractory high‐entropy alloy (RHEA) based on tungsten (e.g. a W‐Ta‐Cr‐V‐Hf composition) can serve as an effective interlayer between tungsten and CuCrZr. Its combined high thermal stability, radiation resistance, and potential to moderate the thermal expansion mismatch between W and CuCrZr make it beneficial for fusion reactor applications.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten component and a CuCrZr heat sink without an interlayer, which exhibit mismatched thermo‐mechanical properties and potential bonding challenges.
generation.intervention: Deposit a thin film interlayer of a nanocrystalline refractory high‐entropy alloy (W‐Ta‐Cr‐V‐Hf) between the W and CuCrZr layers during fabrication.
generation.conditions: Operating conditions typical for fusion reactors, including high temperatures (approximately 1000 K or above), high thermal cycling, and significant irradiation exposure.
generation.structural_mediator: The nano-crystalline structure along with grain refinement behavior under irradiation can facilitate stress accommodation at the W/CuCrZr interface while maintaining phase stability.
generation.mechanism: The RHEA interlayer acts as a graded buffer that minimizes thermal expansion mismatches and enhances interfacial adhesion. Its high configurational entropy and refractory nature impart enhanced radiation tolerance and thermal durability, thus mitigating the degradation typically caused by severe reactor environments.
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved interfacial bonding and reduced residual thermal stresses, leading to enhanced mechanical and irradiation performance compared with direct W/CuCrZr contact.
generation.baseline: Direct bonding of tungsten and CuCrZr, which may suffer from poor thermal expansion compatibility and interfacial degradation under prolonged high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
generation.boundary: The effectiveness of the RHEA interlayer depends on its optimal composition and thickness as well as its chemical compatibility with both tungsten and CuCrZr. Its long-term behavior under cyclic thermal and irradiation exposures needs to be validated.
generation.uncertainty: The optimal deposition process, precise RHEA composition, and long-term interfacial reactions under operational fusion conditions are not yet fully determined, necessitating further experimental validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate test coupons comprising W/RHEA/CuCrZr joints with controlled interlayer thicknesses. Subject these samples to simulated fusion reactor conditions including thermal cycling (from room temperature up to ~1000 K and above) and irradiation exposure (using heavy ion and helium implantation experiments). Compare the performance to samples with direct W/CuCrZr bonding.
measurements: Residual thermal stress (using X-ray diffraction or neutron diffraction)
Microstructural stability and interfacial integrity (using SEM/TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the RHEA interlayer does not significantly enhance the interfacial bonding strength or reduce thermal stresses and if premature degradation or interfacial reaction is observed compared to the direct W/CuCrZr joint, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In the quest of new materials that can withstand severe irradiation and mechanical extremes for advanced applications ( e.g . fission & fusion reactors, space applications, etc.), design, prediction and control of advanced materials beyond current material designs become paramount. Here, through a combined experimental and simulation methodology, we design a nanocrystalline refractory high entropy alloy (RHEA) system. Compositions assessed under extreme environments and in situ electron-microscopy reveal both high thermal stability and radiation resistance. We observe grain refinement under heavy ion irradiation and resistance to dual-beam irradiation and helium implantation in the form of low defect generation and evolution, as well as no detectable grain growth. The experimental and modeling results—showing a good agreement—can be applied to design and rapidly assess other alloys subjected to extreme environmental conditions. Subject terms: Metals and alloys, Power stations
